chapter_theme: The second half of the Thiruvekambamalai (verses 26 to 42) and the unnumbered Thiruvekamba viruttam. The body is a leaking bag and a pot of rice; women are painted bewilderment and a pit of filth; the poet confesses killing, flesh-eating and forgetfulness and asks forgiveness, or asks only to finish his worship before he is killed. Beside the confessions run the rebukes: of flesh-eaters, of those who revile guru, linga and jangama yet want release, of the learned who blame Siva after the fact, of the ungiving and the lustful. The two closing units turn outward: the Lord bears blows from devotees because he has no parents, and the poet asks how many mothers, fathers and births he has had and how many remain.
structure_note: The order is not argued. 264 repeats the closing line of 245; 277 repeats the list of 249; 275 asks of the wicked what 257 asked of the ungiving, ஏன் படைத்தாய். 270 answers 250 with a petition. The last unit (279) is a viruttam of eight lines, not a venba, and closes on கச்சியேகம்ப நாதனே rather than the refrain.

262.reading: Those who do not know the taste of heaven's nectar reckon the taste of a hard fruit to be nectar; so for those who have not a little of the clear knowledge that is honey-nectar, is not the taste of the base nectar good enough?
262.nuance: அமுதம் is said four times and graded: heavenly, the fruit's, the honey of knowledge, and the base (ஈனம்) nectar of worldly pleasure. The last line is irony; the stanza explains rather than condemns why the ignorant are content.

263.reading: The oozing body, the obscene shed, the torn bellows stuffed with flesh, the leather bag into which rice is put, the unspeakable, unstable pot filled with wind: the poet loved it, carried it about and wandered.
263.nuance: Five names for the body, each a container: a shed, a bellows, a bag, a pot. காற்றிற் பொதிந்த, packed with wind, names the breath as what the pot holds and what makes it unstable. The second and third agavals expand the catalogue to dozens of names.

264.reading: The fault that comes by speech, the flaw that comes by thought, the evil deed done, the sins of the glance, the harm of listening to what is not the book of merit: all these and every other fault, forgive.
264.nuance: Faults by speech, thought, deed, sight and hearing: the stanza is the counterpart of 245, which asked forgiveness for what was not done. புண்ணியநூல் அல்லாத கேள்வி counts hearing the wrong book as a sin.

265.reading: Women who grind turmeric without lumps into oil and polish their faces, who put on ornaments and the forehead dot and shine up their brass-leaf earrings, and in broad daylight cast an outward bewilderment: remove my desire for them, the poet asks.
265.nuance: The beauty is manufactured in detail, down to the cheap brass ear-leaf (பித்தளையோலை), and the phrase வெளிமயக்கு from 241 is applied to it; the petition is not that they be punished but that his இட்டம், his liking, be taken away.

266.reading: Born on earth with disease lodged in him, forgetting the great bliss, infatuated with small pleasure, flitting and reeling among base women, seeking gold and giving it to those women: did the Lord command the poet to die so?
266.nuance: பேரின்பம் and சிற்றின்பம், the great bliss and the small pleasure, are the Saiva pair; the stanza's charge is that the second has made him forget the first. The question இறந்திடவோ பணித்தாய் puts the responsibility back on the Lord, as 244 did.

267.reading: Without the elements, without the senses, without the five that they grasp, without difference and quality, without great desire, without before and after, without the inner instruments: in that vision of bliss the poet will stay, his faults cast off.
267.nuance: The negatives strip the tattvas in order: elements, organs, their objects, qualities, desire, time and the கரணங்கள் (mind, intellect, will, ego). காதங்கரணங்கள் is loose for கரணங்கள். What remains is called a காட்சி, a seeing, so the end is not emptiness but bliss seen.

268.reading: Good one, grant me one request: before you kill and throw away this wicked man without knowledge, let the usual worship, the japa, the recitation, the many good observances of the temple and the hymns all be finished, and then kill.
268.nuance: மனு is a petition. The stanza is wry: the poet accepts the killing and bargains only for time to complete the rites, and by listing the rites as what must be finished first he treats them as a debt owed rather than a means. கொல்லுகண்டாய் is an imperative to the Lord.

269.reading: For the sake of the inert pot of a body they seek prey, kill many lives, bite into carcass, sit proud, waste away, and wander eating what they have killed; when Death takes them by the hand and bites them on the left, what will they do?
269.nuance: சடக்கடம் is the body as a lifeless vessel; விடக்கு is flesh as carcass. மிகமெலிந்து (greatly thinned) and படங்கடித்து are hard to construe, and இடக்கடிக்கும் (Death bites on the left, or bites back) is read by sense as Yama returning the bite the eater gave. The argument is retributive: the biter is bitten.

270.reading: The stinking body, the bundle of rice for foxes, the pot the poet fills daily with rice and curry: grant, he asks, that it not fall into the pit from which women's filth and blood flow, but climb out.
270.nuance: The petition answers 250, where the poet said he could not see the bank to climb; here he asks for the climbing (ஏறும்படி). The body and the woman are both described by what flows into and out of them, rice into one, filth from the other.

271.reading: Like thieves who drug a palace, enter and rob it, and then go and petition the kings of the quarters, they revile Siva, revile guru, linga and jangama greatly, and still desire release: what shall the poet say of these great ascetics?
271.nuance: குரு லிங்க சங்கமம் is the Veerasaiva triad of guru, linga and the wandering devotee (jangama), named here as the three things not to revile. எக்குப் பெருந்தவர் is sarcastic. The simile makes reviling the Lord and asking him for release the same act as robbing a king and appealing to kings.

272.reading: Those who will not gladly give plenty of food to the guests who come, yet live in prosperity, and the sinners who do not daily think of praising the name of the one who shares his body with the woman of unsucked breasts: what, asks the poet, is their being on earth?
272.nuance: அருந்தா முலைப் பங்கர், the one who shares (the body) with her whose breasts have never been sucked, names the Lord by Uma as the virgin mother. The stanza sets feeding guests and saying the name side by side as the two duties of a householder.

273.reading: Having learned and known everything, they still do not realise that the Able One knows what is within us; their minds confused, they quarrel in words, grieve according to the fate that closes round them, and afterwards say 'all is Siva's doing'.
273.nuance: The last line can be the learned men's belated excuse, which the stanza mocks, or the poet's own conclusion, which the learned reach too late; the Tamil allows both. Read the first way the stanza is about blaming fate after one's own folly; read the second, it agrees with 290 and 294 that nothing is done apart from the Lord. எல்லாம் அறிந்து படித்தே is the recurring Siddhar target of book-learning.

274.reading: They think of gold and seek it hard, they think of the flower-like woman and melt for her; the wretches on this earth who do not think of you and do not worship you, why, the poet asks, have you kept them here for me to see?
274.nuance: நினைந்து three times: the stanza is about what thought is spent on. உலுத்தர் is a strong word, misers or wretches. என்னை இருந்து கண்டாய் may mean 'why have you made me see them' or 'what have you seen in them'; the first fits the series of ஏன் questions.

275.reading: Harsh-tongued idlers, the base, gluttons, lechers, utter fools who do cruel sin, who grow in this world like tall palmyras without knowing the way of the good: why, the poet asks, did the Lord make such troublesome people?
275.nuance: நெடும்பனை போல, like a tall palmyra, is growth without use, as the palm gives nothing to those at its foot; the question ஏன் வகுத்தாய் repeats 257's ஏன் படைத்தாய். இடும்பர், people who are இடும்பை, trouble, is the poet's coinage.

276.reading: The poet killed many lives, then killed and killed again and ate, and did harm besides; saying 'let that end', he stood in the Lord's presence, trusting that for that reason the Lord would bear the fault.
276.nuance: The confession is specific (killing and eating) and the ground of hope is only standing before the Lord (நின்சன்னிதிக்கே நின்றேன்); no penance is offered. Set beside 269, the poet counts himself among the flesh-eaters he threatened with Death's bite.

277.reading: What if there is a town, what if there are good people, people of name who help, the mother who bore one, the tender wife, glory, distinction, beauty, in this country: what of it, Lord?
277.nuance: The list of 249 returns with இருந்தென்ன, 'what if it is there', so that the question is no longer whether these last but whether they are of any use. வல்லாய் (able one) is the Lord as the only one who can answer.

278.reading: To be struck with a bow, kicked with a sandal, pelted with a stone by one in anger, beaten with a cane: is it not because the Dancer of Tillai, whose groves hum with bees, has no mother and father?
278.nuance: The four blows are the devotees' legends: Arjuna's bow, Kannappar's sandal, Sakkiyar's stones and the cane of the Pandya's overseer on the Lord who carried earth at Madurai. The joke is that the Lord submits as an orphan does, with no parents to object; underneath it is the doctrine that he is unborn (அன்னைபிதா இல்லாதவன்) and that love from his devotees is received in whatever form it takes.

279.reading: How many mothers and how many fathers, how many wives and how many children, how many births before: the fool did not know; and how many births are still to come? What is he to do, Lord of Ekambam at Kachi?
279.nuance: எத்தனை எத்தனை eleven times; the relations the earlier stanzas called impermanent are here multiplied across births so that no single mother or wife is one's own. The count forward (இன்னம் எத்தனை) is the only question with weight.

links.note: Both heap names of containers on the body: Arunagirinathar's bag fed by the two deeds, pot where stench pools and hut the life moves out of; Pattinathar's shed, torn bellows, leather bag fed with rice and pot of wind. Both confess to having loved it; Arunagirinathar asks to give up the delusion that it will not perish.

The same closing line, எல்லாப் பிழையும் பொறுத்தருள்வாய்: 245 lists what the poet did not do (learn, melt, meditate, say the five letters, praise, worship), 264 what he did by speech, thought, deed, glance and hearing. Together they make a full confession of omission and commission.

Both watch women at their toilet, turmeric, dots, earrings and the rest, and name the finished beauty as what undoes men; Arunagirinathar asks for the feet to end his desire, Pattinathar asks that his liking (இட்டம்) for them be removed.

Tirumular says to set the five states in nada and the rest, put the corpse-like mala behind and seek the king beyond mind and speech; Pattinathar describes a vision of bliss without elements, senses, objects, qualities, time or the inner instruments. Both reach the end by subtraction of the tattvas.

The Naladiyar says the bellies of the senseless are burning grounds for the beasts and birds they eat; Pattinathar's flesh-eaters feed the inert pot of the body with killed lives and are themselves bitten by Death. Both make the eater's body a place of the dead.

Sivavakkiyar says that even if you kill one creature with another and make it your food, and lie and steal in the market, lovingly joining the Lord brings the gods within you that day; Pattinathar says those who kill and eat will have no answer when Death seizes them. The conflict holds on the plain reading of 1239, where joining the Lord overrides the deed; on its softer reading, that sinners are not shut out, Pattinathar's own 276 agrees with it.

250 said the poet had been thrown into the pit from which filth and blood pour and could not see the bank to climb out; 270 names the same pit and asks the Lord for the climbing. The complaint becomes a petition.

The Naladiyar's fool calls a pot that seeps filth from nine openings 'broad-shouldered one'; Pattinathar calls his own body a pot of rice and curry and the woman's body a pit of filth and blood. Both strip the body to a vessel of waste; the Naladiyar aims it at the lover's eye, Pattinathar at both bodies at once.

The Kural says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods anxiously and then say they have no support; Pattinathar asks what being on earth is worth for those who will not feed the guests who come yet live in prosperity. Both treat hospitality as the test of a household.

257 asked why the Lord created men who give nothing, like fruitless trees and dry tanks; 275 asks why he made the harsh, the lustful and the cruel, who grow like tall palmyras without knowing the good. The same question widens from the ungiving to the wicked.

The same catalogue, town, kin, name, women, children, glory, wealth; 249 says none of it lasts and only the feet do, 277 asks what use any of it is even while it lasts. The second stanza drops the affirmation and keeps the question.

Tirumular says the kin who cling and follow are worse than one's deeds and that the road of rebirth can be closed by lighting awareness while in the body; Pattinathar counts the mothers, fathers, wives and children of uncounted births and asks how many more. Both treat kin as the recurring content of birth rather than its consolation.

source_issues: 263 line 2 is spaced பீற்றற் து ருத்தியைச் for பீற்றற் துருத்தியைச்.
267 line 3 காதங்கரணங்களும் is loose for கரணங்களும்; the metre may have required the extra syllable.
279 (thiruvekambamalai:u1) is unnumbered in the source and headed திருவேகம்பவிருத்தம்; it is a viruttam appended to the venba sequence and not part of the forty-two.
